slides.body: The model breaks for the fifth cause.

slides.direction: The root-cause box of section 17.12.
slides.text:
Observed behavior : Pull request 2 lists the three commits of pull request 1 again, shows their
                    changes again, and conflicts with main in router/priority.py.
Git state         : merge-base(main, branch) is still 9a383e5, the original fork point.
                    main's tip 1b2b8ed has one parent, 9aa221a.
Mechanism         : The squash commit copied the content of the branch and recorded no link to it.
                    For Git, 44c1e7b, 12ae95d and 16d4788 were never merged. base..head lists them.
                    The three-way merge sees "both sides added router/priority.py since 9a383e5,
                    with different content": an add/add conflict.
Root cause        : Content merged without ancestry (Chapter 8, section 8.12), then more work on top
                    of the old ancestry.
Why Git does this : The merge base comes from parent links only. Git never compares patches to
                    guess that a commit "is already there".
Correct fix       : Transplant the new commits onto main: git rebase --onto origin/main <last squashed commit>.
Prevention        : Delete the head branch after a squash or rebase merge and start new work from
                    main. Enable automatic deletion of head branches in the repository.

lines.s: # Ravi. One commit of his own, on a branch he created from main:
* a1ae0eb Accept tickets without a subject
* 29be88c Describe how to run the tests
# The pull request was opened with base release/1.0. What it lists and shows:
a1ae0eb Accept tickets without a subject
29be88c Describe how to run the tests
# Which base makes this branch a one-commit pull request?
for b in origin/main origin/release/1.0; do echo "$b: $(git rev-list --count $b..fix/empty-subject)
29be88c Describe how to run the tests
# Fix A: the change belongs on main after all. Same branch, other base:
a1ae0eb Accept tickets without a subject
# Fix B: the change does belong on release/1.0. Move the one commit there:
| * 29be88c Describe how to run the tests

slides.body: Create a second long-lived branch in your practice repository, for example a release branch from an older commit, and open a pull request from a branch that was created from main against that release branch.
Then apply fix A on the platform:

items: Continuing on a branch after its pull request was squash-merged. Root cause: the squash commit has no parent link to the branch, so the merge base never moved and the old commits are listed again.
Fixing a wrong-base pull request with a plain git rebase <base>. Root cause: it replays every commit, the foreign ones included; --onto with the right upstream selects only your commits.
Changing the base when the branch started in the wrong place, or the reverse. Root cause: the two repairs answer different questions: where the change belongs, and where the work began.
Opening a pull request without looking at the range. Root cause: gh pr create uses the default branch as base unless told otherwise.
Trusting the "Files changed" tab to be complete on a very large pull request. Root cause: display limits and .gitattributes rules hide files that git diff --stat base...head shows.

slides.lead: You should now be able to say:
items: A pull request that shows too much has a head with commits the base does not reach, or a base the work did not start from.
The five documented causes are: reuse after a squash merge, a wrong or changed base, a base that moved, rewritten history, and truncated or hidden diffs.
git merge-base and git rev-list --count base..head test the first two.
A wrong base is fixed by changing the base or by git rebase --onto, depending on where the change belongs.
After a squash merge the branch's commits are not ancestors of the base; delete the branch and start from main.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Two videos ago you learned the sentence that the whole chapter hangs on. A pull request, a proposal to merge a head branch into a base branch, shows base..head in its commit list and base...head in its diff. And everything is computed from three commits: the tip of the base, the tip of the head, and their merge base, the most recent commit that both histories contain.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Two videos ago you learned the sentence that the whole chapter hangs on. A pull request, a proposal to merge a head branch into a base branch, shows `base..head` in its commit list and `base...head` in its diff. And everything is computed from three commits: the tip of the base, the tip of the head, and their merge base, the most recent commit that both histories contain.

beats.text: So every surprise on a pull request page is a surprise about one of those three. Either the head contains commits that the base does not reach, or the base is not the branch the work started from. That is section 17.12 in one sentence, and this video is that section.
beats.tele: So every surprise on a pull request page is a surprise about one of those three. Either the head contains commits that the base does not reach, or the base is not the branch the work started from. That is section 17.12 in one sentence, and this video is that section.

beats.text: GitHub documents five causes. The first two can be reproduced in plain Git, and they are the two replays: labs/ch17/wrong-base.sh and labs/ch17/squash-reuse.sh. Then a walkthrough following Lab 21.2 on a practice repository.
beats.tele: GitHub documents five causes. The first two can be reproduced in plain Git, and they are the two replays: `labs/ch17/wrong-base.sh` and `labs/ch17/squash-reuse.sh`. Then a walkthrough following Lab 21.2 on a practice repository.

beats.text: Labels: git rebase --onto is 🟡 CAUTION: it rewrites the current branch. Preview with git log <upstream>..HEAD. Recover with ORIG_HEAD, the reflog, or git rebase --abort. Republishing a rewritten branch needs git push --force-with-lease, 🔴 DANGEROUS, with the five answers from the last video: appropriate for your own pull request branch after a rebase. gh pr edit --base is 🟡: it changes the base and can dismiss approvals.
beats.tele: Labels: `git rebase --onto` is 🟡 CAUTION: it rewrites the current branch. Preview with `git log <upstream>..HEAD`. Recover with `ORIG_HEAD`, the reflog, or `git rebase --abort`. Republishing a rewritten branch needs `git push --force-with-lease`, 🔴 DANGEROUS, with the five answers from the last video: appropriate for your own pull request branch after a rebase. `gh pr edit --base` is 🟡: it changes the base and can dismiss approvals.

beats.text: After this video you can:
beats.tele: After this video you can:

beats.text: Give the documented causes of a pull request with many unrelated commits or files.
beats.tele: Give the documented causes of a pull request with many unrelated commits or files.

beats.text: Diagnose a pull request opened against the wrong base and fix it by changing the base or by transplanting the branch.
beats.tele: Diagnose a pull request opened against the wrong base and fix it by changing the base or by transplanting the branch.

beats.text: Explain why a branch reused after a squash merge lists its old commits again and may conflict.
beats.tele: Explain why a branch reused after a squash merge lists its old commits again and may conflict.

beats.text: Repair the reused branch with git rebase --onto.
beats.tele: Repair the reused branch with `git rebase --onto`.

beats.text: Name the Git command that tests each cause.
beats.tele: Name the Git command that tests each cause.

beats.text: Cause one: the head branch was reused after a squash merge, the merge that replaces your commits by one new commit. You see commits that were "already squashed" listed again, and repeated conflicts. The mechanism: the squash commit has no parent link to the branch, so the merge base never moved.
beats.tele: Cause one: the head branch was reused after a squash merge, the merge that replaces your commits by one new commit. You see commits that were "already squashed" listed again, and repeated conflicts. The mechanism: the squash commit has no parent link to the branch, so the merge base never moved.

beats.text: Cause two: a wrong or changed base branch. You see every commit of the branch the work was really based on. The mechanism: the range is taken against a base that does not contain those commits.
beats.tele: Cause two: a wrong or changed base branch. You see every commit of the branch the work was really based on. The mechanism: the range is taken against a base that does not contain those commits.

beats.text: Cause three: the base branch moved. The pull request page and a compare page disagree, because they "can calculate changed files from different merge bases". Nothing is wrong. If the two must agree, update the branch.
beats.tele: Cause three: the base branch moved. The pull request page and a compare page disagree, because they "can calculate changed files from different merge bases". Nothing is wrong. If the two must agree, update the branch.

beats.text: Cause four: rewritten or force-pushed history. You see old and new copies of commits and outdated review comments. GitHub's words: "Force pushing rewrites repository history and can ... corrupt pull requests." And if someone force-pushes the base branch, every open pull request against it lists the removed commits. That is a reason to block force pushes on shared branches.
beats.tele: Cause four: rewritten or force-pushed history. You see old and new copies of commits and outdated review comments. GitHub's words: "Force pushing rewrites repository history and can ... corrupt pull requests." And if someone force-pushes the base branch, every open pull request against it lists the removed commits. That is a reason to block force pushes on shared branches.

beats.text: Cause five: the diff is truncated or hidden. Files are missing from "Files changed" because of display limits, or because a .gitattributes rule hides the file. The file changed and the page does not render it. git diff --stat base...head on your machine has no such limit.
beats.tele: Cause five: the diff is truncated or hidden. Files are missing from "Files changed" because of display limits, or because a `.gitattributes` rule hides the file. The file changed and the page does not render it. `git diff --stat base...head` on your machine has no such limit.

beats.text: Now the two causes that deserve a mechanism.
beats.tele: Now the two causes that deserve a mechanism.

beats.text: The wrong base. On screen is today's example: a branch created from main, for a fix meant for a release branch. Why does it happen? Because people create branches from main by habit, and open the pull request against wherever the fix is meant to go. If those are two different branches, the range base..head contains everything on main that the release branch does not have. Merging such a pull request would carry unreleased work into the release branch.
beats.tele: The wrong base. On screen is today's example: a branch created from `main`, for a fix meant for a release branch. Why does it happen? Because people create branches from `main` by habit, and open the pull request against wherever the fix is meant to go. If those are two different branches, the range `base..head` contains everything on `main` that the release branch does not have. Merging such a pull request would carry unreleased work into the release branch.

beats.text: There are two repairs, and they are not interchangeable. If the base is wrong, change the base of the pull request. GitHub warns about the side effect: "some commits may be removed from the timeline. Review comments may also become outdated." If the base is right and the branch started in the wrong place, transplant the commits with git rebase --onto. A plain git rebase onto the release branch would replay every commit, the foreign ones included, and change nothing about the pull request except the commit IDs.
beats.tele: There are two repairs, and they are not interchangeable. If the base is wrong, change the base of the pull request. GitHub warns about the side effect: "some commits may be removed from the timeline. Review comments may also become outdated." If the base is right and the branch started in the wrong place, transplant the commits with `git rebase --onto`. A plain `git rebase` onto the release branch would replay every commit, the foreign ones included, and change nothing about the pull request except the commit IDs.

beats.text: Quick quiz. In our picture the fix really is for the release. Which repair? A: change the base. B: transplant the branch. Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. In our picture the fix really is for the release. Which repair? A: change the base. B: transplant the branch. Your answer?

beats.text: B. The base is right, and the branch started in the wrong place. So the one commit moves, and gets a new ID.
beats.tele: B. The base is right, and the branch started in the wrong place. So the one commit moves, and gets a new ID.

beats.text: Squash, then reuse. On screen: main after a squash merge, and the branch that was squashed. This one needs the internals of the merge base, which you learned in the merge videos. The merge base comes from parent links only. Git never compares patches to guess that a commit "is already there".
beats.tele: Squash, then reuse. On screen: `main` after a squash merge, and the branch that was squashed. This one needs the internals of the merge base, which you learned in the merge videos. The merge base comes from parent links only. Git never compares patches to guess that a commit "is already there".

beats.text: A squash merge creates one new commit on the base that copies the content of the branch and records no link to it. So after the squash, for Git, the branch's commits were never merged. The merge base of main and the old branch is still the original fork point.
beats.tele: A squash merge creates one new commit on the base that copies the content of the branch and records no link to it. So after the squash, for Git, the branch's commits were never merged. The merge base of `main` and the old branch is still the original fork point.

beats.text: Keep working on that branch, and two things follow. The range base..head lists the old commits again. And the three-way merge sees that both sides added the same files since the fork point, with different content: a conflict in a file that only you ever edited.
beats.tele: Keep working on that branch, and two things follow. The range `base..head` lists the old commits again. And the three-way merge sees that both sides added the same files since the fork point, with different content: a conflict in a file that only you ever edited.

beats.text: GitHub's page says the same: "If you keep working on the same head branch after a squash merge, later pull requests can include commits that were already squashed into the base branch."
beats.tele: GitHub's page says the same: "If you keep working on the same head branch after a squash merge, later pull requests can include commits that were already squashed into the base branch."

beats.text: Three ways out. One: move only what is new, with git rebase --onto origin/main <last squashed commit>. Two: merge main into the branch and resolve once, which moves the merge base. Three, the prevention: a new branch from main for every pull request, and automatic deletion of head branches, set by gh repo edit --delete-branch-on-merge.
beats.tele: Three ways out. One: move only what is new, with `git rebase --onto origin/main <last squashed commit>`. Two: merge `main` into the branch and resolve once, which moves the merge base. Three, the prevention: a new branch from `main` for every pull request, and automatic deletion of head branches, set by `gh repo edit --delete-branch-on-merge`.

beats.text: When not to transplant: when other people have based work on the branch. A rebase replaces its commits, and the push must be forced.
beats.tele: When not to transplant: when other people have based work on the branch. A rebase replaces its commits, and the push must be forced.

beats.text: Think of the page as a ruler laid between two points, the merge base and the head. Everything between the points is shown. When the page shows too much, don't stare at what is shown. Ask where the left end of the ruler is.
beats.tele: Think of the page as a ruler laid between two points, the merge base and the head. Everything between the points is shown. When the page shows too much, don't stare at what is shown. Ask where the left end of the ruler is.

beats.text: Try it now, thirty seconds, on paper: draw a branch that was squashed and then reused, and mark where the ruler starts. I'll wait.

beats.text: git merge-base base head tells you. If the left end is further back than you expected, there are only two reasons. The head carries history that the base never received as history: that is squash-then-reuse, where the content arrived and the ancestry did not. Or you are measuring against the wrong base: that is the wrong-base case.

beats.text: The model breaks for the fifth cause. Truncated and hidden diffs are a property of the page, not of the range. There the ruler is right and the display is short.

beats.tele: The lower line is the branch: the three commits of pull request 1, still there, and one new commit on top.

beats.text: Now lay the ruler. The merge base is 9a383e5, at the far left. Between it and the head are four commits. That's the question from the hook, answered: the range starts further back than the author thought.

beats.text: And the repair: the one new commit, replayed on main, with a new ID.
beats.tele: And the repair: the one new commit, replayed on `main`, with a new ID.

beats.text: Ravi created the branch fix/empty-subject from main, by habit. The fix is meant for the release branch, so he opened the pull request with base release/1.0.
beats.tele: Ravi created the branch `fix/empty-subject` from `main`, by habit. The fix is meant for the release branch, so he opened the pull request with base `release/1.0`.

beats.tele: One commit of his own. What will the pull request against `release/1.0` list?

beats.tele: Fix A: the change belongs on `main` after all. Same branch, other base.

beats.text: On GitHub that is gh pr edit --base main. Nothing in Git changes. The pull request object gets a different base, and the same branch is a one-commit pull request.

beats.tele: Fix B: the change does belong on `release/1.0`. Move the one commit there.

beats.tele: The branch was rewritten, so republishing it is a forced push, with `--force-with-lease`, on Ravi's own pull request branch.

beats.text: The branch of pull request 1 is still here: it was squash-merged, and nobody deleted it.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Continuing on a branch after its pull request was squash-merged. Root cause: the squash commit has no parent link to the branch, so the merge base never moved and the old commits are listed again.
beats.tele: Continuing on a branch after its pull request was squash-merged. Root cause: the squash commit has no parent link to the branch, so the merge base never moved and the old commits are listed again.

beats.text: Fixing a wrong-base pull request with a plain git rebase <base>. Root cause: it replays every commit, the foreign ones included; --onto with the right upstream selects only your commits.
beats.tele: Fixing a wrong-base pull request with a plain `git rebase <base>`. Root cause: it replays every commit, the foreign ones included; `--onto` with the right upstream selects only your commits.

beats.text: Changing the base when the branch started in the wrong place, or the reverse. Root cause: the two repairs answer different questions: where the change belongs, and where the work began.
beats.tele: Changing the base when the branch started in the wrong place, or the reverse. Root cause: the two repairs answer different questions: where the change belongs, and where the work began.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. An ML platform team maintains main and a release/2.4 branch for a customer deployment. An engineer fixes a tokenizer bug for the release, branches from main by habit, and opens the pull request against release/2.4. The page shows 212 commits and several hundred files. The reviewer refuses to look at it, correctly.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. An ML platform team maintains `main` and a `release/2.4` branch for a customer deployment. An engineer fixes a tokenizer bug for the release, branches from `main` by habit, and opens the pull request against `release/2.4`. The page shows 212 commits and several hundred files. The reviewer refuses to look at it, correctly.

beats.text: The engineer runs the diagnosis from this video: the count of commits against each candidate base. One against main, 212 against the release branch. The base is right, the fix is needed in the release, so the branch started in the wrong place: fix B. One git rebase --onto origin/release/2.4 origin/main, one check of the range, one push with --force-with-lease, and the pull request is one commit.

beats.text: Question 263 of the CTO question bank:
beats.tele: Question 263 of the CTO question bank:

beats.text: Answer out loud. A strong answer starts from what the commit list is, as a Git range, and then gives causes as statements about the endpoints of that range, not as a list of anecdotes. For each cause it names the command that confirms it. It treats squash-then-reuse with the mechanism of the merge base, and it distinguishes the two repairs for a wrong base.

beats.text: Let's land this. When a pull request shows too much, you now ask one thing first: where does the range start?
beats.tele: Let's land this. When a pull request shows too much, you now ask one thing first: where does the range start?

beats.text: You should now be able to say:
beats.tele: You should now be able to say:

beats.text: A pull request that shows too much has a head with commits the base does not reach, or a base the work did not start from.
beats.tele: A pull request that shows too much has a head with commits the base does not reach, or a base the work did not start from.

beats.text: The five documented causes are: reuse after a squash merge, a wrong or changed base, a base that moved, rewritten history, and truncated or hidden diffs.
beats.tele: The five documented causes are: reuse after a squash merge, a wrong or changed base, a base that moved, rewritten history, and truncated or hidden diffs.

beats.text: git merge-base and git rev-list --count base..head test the first two.
beats.tele: `git merge-base` and `git rev-list --count base..head` test the first two.

beats.text: A wrong base is fixed by changing the base or by git rebase --onto, depending on where the change belongs.
beats.tele: A wrong base is fixed by changing the base or by `git rebase --onto`, depending on where the change belongs.

beats.text: After a squash merge the branch's commits are not ancestors of the base; delete the branch and start from main.
beats.tele: After a squash merge the branch's commits are not ancestors of the base; delete the branch and start from `main`.
